meta.name: CompTIA Project+ (PK0-005)
meta.notes: Initial publication. Covers the four PK0-005 domains: Project Management Concepts (33%), Project Life Cycle Phases (30%), Tools and Documentation (19%), and Basics of IT and Governance (18%). Correct positions spread 3/3/3/3 with no adjacent repeats. Options are option-length-parity balanced within each question; distractors are plausible peers rather than obvious wrongs.

questions.question: A team is starting a new internal SaaS product where the requirements are expected to evolve every two-week cadence based on stakeholder feedback. Which development approach BEST fits this situation?
options: Predictive (waterfall) — a single, sequential plan is baselined up front and changes are actively discouraged after approval
Adaptive (agile) — scope evolves through short iterations that deliver working increments and re-prioritise the backlog every cycle
Purely incremental with a fixed scope — the whole product is delivered in identical time-boxed chunks with no scope re-planning
Extreme predictive — every requirement is signed off before any design work and no re-planning is scheduled
questions.explanation: Adaptive (agile) methods are designed for projects whose requirements are expected to change: short iterations produce working increments and the backlog is re-prioritised each cycle, which is exactly the two-week feedback loop described. Predictive (waterfall) baselines scope, schedule and cost up front and treats change as an exception — a poor fit when change is the norm. A purely incremental approach that never re-plans still forces the team to lock scope, giving up the very benefit the question asks for. 'Extreme predictive' is not a real methodology and would compound the problem by forbidding re-planning entirely.

questions.question: During a workshop the project manager is assigning ownership of tasks so that every activity has exactly one person Accountable while several people can be Responsible or Consulted. Which tool is the manager producing?
options: A work breakdown structure (WBS) — a hierarchical decomposition of deliverables into work packages
A stakeholder register — a catalogue of stakeholders, their interests, influence and communication preferences
A RACI matrix — a chart mapping tasks to Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed roles
A risk register — a log of identified risks with probability, impact, response and owner
questions.explanation: A RACI matrix maps each activity to who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed, and the rule that exactly one Accountable exists per row is the diagnostic property of RACI. A WBS decomposes deliverables into work packages but does not assign role types. A stakeholder register captures interests and influence rather than task-level accountability. A risk register tracks probability, impact and response for identified risks and has no per-task R/A/C/I column.

questions.question: A sponsor asks for the earliest date on which the project can finish if every activity starts as soon as its predecessors are done. Which schedule technique produces this date and the sequence that drives it?
options: Monte Carlo simulation — probabilistic modelling that outputs a distribution of finish dates for the whole project
Resource levelling — adjusts start and finish dates to remove over-allocation of shared resources
Rolling-wave planning — plans near-term work in detail and defers detailed planning for later work
Critical path method (CPM) — computes the longest zero-float path through the network and yields the earliest finish
questions.explanation: The Critical Path Method walks the network forwards and backwards to find the longest chain of zero-float activities; that chain's total duration is the project's earliest possible finish date and any slip on it slips the project. Monte Carlo simulation gives a probability distribution over finish dates but requires an underlying schedule and does not by itself identify the driving path. Resource levelling reshuffles dates to fix over-allocation and can lengthen the schedule rather than reveal its earliest finish. Rolling-wave planning is a planning cadence — plan the near term in detail, later work at a high level — not a duration-calculation technique.

questions.question: A stakeholder submits a scope change midway through execution. According to standard change control, what MUST happen before the team implements the change?
options: The change is captured, its impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk is assessed, and a change control board approves or rejects it
The project manager implements the change immediately and then updates the plan retroactively if time permits
The team implements the change only if the sponsor's verbal approval is obtained during a hallway conversation
The change is added to the backlog and worked whenever there is spare capacity, with no formal impact analysis
questions.explanation: Formal change control captures the request, performs an impact assessment across scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk, and routes it to the change control board (CCB) or delegated authority for an approve/reject decision before any work starts. Implementing first and updating the plan later loses traceability and defeats the point of a baseline. Verbal hallway approval creates no audit trail and violates the CCB's charter. Silently backlogging a change with no impact analysis bypasses the process entirely and lets scope drift without visibility.

questions.question: The project charter is being drafted. Which of the following is the PRIMARY purpose of that document?
options: It captures the day-to-day task assignments and daily stand-up notes for the delivery team
It formally authorises the project, names the project manager and grants them authority to apply organisational resources
It defines the detailed technical architecture and interface specifications for the deliverable
It records the closing lessons learned and archives them in the organisational process assets
questions.explanation: The project charter formally authorises the project's existence, names the project manager, states the high-level objectives and success criteria, and grants the PM authority to apply organisational resources. Daily task assignments live in the schedule and stand-up notes, not the charter. Detailed technical architecture is produced later during planning and design and is not part of the initiating document. Lessons learned are collected and archived during closing, long after the charter has served its purpose.

questions.question: A project is closing. The customer has accepted the final deliverable and the contract is being closed out. Which activity is MOST characteristic of the closing phase?
options: Baselining scope, schedule and cost for the first time so the team knows what to build
Selecting the sellers and awarding the procurement contracts for the work packages
Obtaining formal sign-off, releasing resources and documenting lessons learned for future projects
Executing the majority of the work packages that produce the product of the project
questions.explanation: Closing includes obtaining formal customer sign-off (acceptance) on the deliverable, closing procurements, releasing the team and vendors, and capturing lessons learned into the organisation's process assets so future projects benefit. Baselining scope, schedule and cost is a planning activity. Selecting sellers and awarding procurement contracts happens during executing (guided by planning), not closing. Executing the bulk of the work packages is by definition the executing phase, not closing.

questions.question: A sprint retrospective just ended and the team has agreed on two process improvements to try next sprint. Where do these improvements MOST appropriately go?
options: They are written into the signed project charter as new authorising clauses for the sponsor to countersign
They are archived in the organisational process assets and revisited only at project closure
They are logged in the risk register as new threats with probability and impact scores
They are added to the next sprint's plan as concrete, owned actions the team commits to trying
questions.explanation: Retrospective outcomes are only valuable if the team acts on them, so agreed improvements should be added to the next sprint's plan as concrete, owned actions with a clear owner. The charter is an authorising document, not a place for iterative process tweaks, and reopening it every sprint would be inappropriate. Archiving improvements for review only at closure defeats the retrospective's purpose of enabling continuous improvement now. The risk register captures threats and opportunities with probability and impact scores, not agreed process actions.

questions.question: Which document establishes the mutual, legally binding obligations between the project's organisation and an external vendor supplying specialised equipment?
options: A statement of work (SOW) alone — an internal description of the work with no signatures required
A contract (for example a fixed-price agreement) — a signed, legally enforceable instrument between the parties
A memorandum of understanding (MOU) — a non-binding expression of intent between the parties
A request for information (RFI) — a market-sounding document asking vendors about capabilities
questions.explanation: A contract (fixed-price, cost-reimbursable or time-and-materials) is the signed, legally enforceable instrument that binds the parties to their obligations for supplying the equipment. A statement of work describes the scope of work but is typically an attachment to a contract, not itself the binding instrument. An MOU records a non-binding expression of intent and cannot be enforced as a supply agreement. An RFI collects capability information from the market to shape a later procurement and creates no binding obligation.

questions.question: A stakeholder analysis rates a manager as having HIGH power over the project and LOW interest in it. According to the power/interest grid, which engagement strategy fits?
options: Manage closely — invest the largest share of engagement effort because they are both influential and highly interested
Monitor only — the lowest engagement level, appropriate for stakeholders with little power and little interest
Keep informed — regular detailed updates suit stakeholders whose interest is high but whose formal power is low
Keep satisfied — enough targeted engagement to prevent them becoming blockers, without over-communicating
questions.explanation: In the power/interest grid, high-power / low-interest stakeholders should be Kept Satisfied: enough targeted engagement to keep them supportive without flooding them with detail they do not want, so they do not become blockers. Manage Closely is reserved for high-power / high-interest stakeholders. Monitor is for the low-power / low-interest quadrant. Keep Informed applies to low-power / high-interest stakeholders who want detail but cannot themselves derail the project.

questions.question: At a checkpoint the project's earned value (EV) is 80 and the actual cost (AC) is 100. What does the cost performance index (CPI) tell the project manager about efficiency, and what number results?
options: CPI = 0.80 — the project has earned only 80 cents of value per dollar spent, so it is running over budget
CPI = 1.25 — the project is earning 1.25 dollars of value per dollar spent, so it is running under budget
CPI = 20 — the project has 20 units of positive cost variance and is comfortably ahead on cost
CPI = -0.20 — the project has negative cost efficiency and every dollar spent destroys 20 cents of value
questions.explanation: CPI is defined as EV divided by AC, so 80 divided by 100 equals 0.80, meaning the project earns 80 cents of value per dollar spent — clearly over budget. 1.25 would be AC/EV inverted, which is not the CPI formula. 20 is the cost variance (EV minus AC would give −20 here) rather than an efficiency index. CPI is a ratio and cannot be negative because EV and AC are both non-negative amounts.

questions.question: The team decides to buy cyber-insurance covering a specific breach scenario the project could trigger. Under standard risk response classifications, which strategy has been applied?
options: Avoid — the plan has been rewritten so the triggering scenario cannot occur at all
Mitigate — the probability or the impact of the risk has been reduced through preventive controls
Transfer — the financial consequence of the risk has been shifted to a third party such as an insurer
Accept — the risk has been acknowledged with no proactive action other than a contingency reserve
questions.explanation: Buying insurance for a specific breach scenario shifts the financial consequence to a third party, which is the textbook definition of Transfer. Avoid would remove the risk entirely by re-planning so the scenario cannot occur — insurance does not prevent the breach itself. Mitigate reduces the probability or impact through preventive controls such as encryption or MFA. Accept means acknowledging the risk without proactive action, at most funding a contingency reserve to absorb its cost if it happens.

questions.question: A regulated project handles cardholder data on behalf of an EU retailer. Which compliance pairing MUST be reflected in the project's governance controls?
options: GDPR for the personal-data protection obligations, plus PCI DSS for the cardholder-data security controls
HIPAA for the personal-data protection obligations, plus SOX for the cardholder-data security controls
GDPR for the personal-data protection obligations, plus HIPAA for the cardholder-data security controls
SOX for the personal-data protection obligations, plus GDPR for the cardholder-data security controls
questions.explanation: GDPR governs the processing of personal data of individuals in the EU, and PCI DSS is the payment-card-industry standard specifically covering cardholder data — the correct pairing for an EU retailer's project handling cardholder data. HIPAA is US healthcare-specific and does not apply to EU retail personal data. SOX governs US public-company financial reporting controls; it is not a cardholder-data or personal-data privacy framework. Using HIPAA for cardholder data or GDPR as a cardholder-data security standard misidentifies each framework's actual scope.
